title: Explain the Decomposition design pattern (by business capability, by subdomain/DDD, by transaction, by scalability).

s1_definition.profdef: The Decomposition pattern is the set of strategies for deciding where to draw service boundaries when breaking a system into microservices. The four main strategies are: decompose by business capability, where each service maps to a thing the business does, such as Payments or Lending; decompose by subdomain using Domain-Driven Design, where each service maps to a bounded context in the domain model; decompose by transaction, where operations that must share a consistency boundary stay in one service; and decompose by scalability, where a component with very different load is split out so it can scale on its own. Good decomposition maximizes cohesion inside a service and minimizes coupling between services.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, decomposition is deciding how to divide one giant bank into departments. By business capability means one department per job the bank does: a Payments department, a Loans department, a Cards department. By subdomain (DDD) means dividing along how the business actually thinks and speaks, so the people who talk about "sanctioning" and "EMI" form the Loan department. By transaction means keeping things that must balance together in one room, so debit and credit of a single ledger entry are not split. By scalability means the festival-season payments counter, which gets slammed, is given its own building so it can add tellers without the quiet loans desk growing too.
s1_definition.oneliner: Decompose by business capability or DDD subdomain for clear ownership, keep tightly coupled transactions in one service, and split by scalability when one part has very different load, always maximizing cohesion and minimizing coupling.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Decomposition pattern is the set of strategies for deciding where to draw service boundaries when breaking a system into microservices. The four main strategies are: decompose by business capability, where each service maps to a thing the business does, such as Payments or Lending; decompose by subdomain using Domain-Driven Design, where each service maps to a bounded context in the domain model; decompose by transaction, where operations that must share a consistency boundary stay in one service; and decompose by scalability, where a component with very different load is split out so it can scale on its own. Good decomposition maximizes cohesion inside a service and minimizes coupling between services.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, decomposition is deciding how to divide one giant bank into departments. By business capability means one department per job the bank does: a Payments department, a Loans department, a Cards department. By subdomain (DDD) means dividing along how the business actually thinks and speaks, so the people who talk about "sanctioning" and "EMI" form the Loan department. By transaction means keeping things that must balance together in one room, so debit and credit of a single ledger entry are not split. By scalability means the festival-season payments counter, which gets slammed, is given its own building so it can add tellers without the quiet loans desk growing too.

**One line to remember:** Decompose by business capability or DDD subdomain for clear ownership, keep tightly coupled transactions in one service, and split by scalability when one part has very different load, always maximizing cohesion and minimizing coupling.

sections.s2_technical:
Decompose by business capability means each service owns a capability the business offers. You list what the bank does, such as managing accounts, making payments, approving loans, and sending notifications, and each becomes a service. The boundary is stable because business capabilities change slowly, and ownership is clear because a team can own "payments" end to end. In code this shows up as a `PaymentService` that handles everything about payments and nothing about loans.

Decompose by subdomain using DDD is a refinement that uses the domain model to find boundaries. A bounded context is a region where a term has one precise meaning, so "account" in the Lending context might mean a loan account while "account" in the Deposits context means a savings account. Each bounded context becomes a service, and the ubiquitous language inside it stays consistent. This avoids the trap of one giant shared "Account" model that tries to mean everything to everyone.

Decompose by transaction keeps operations that must be atomic together inside one service. If two pieces of data must always change together under one consistency boundary, splitting them forces a saga and eventual consistency, which adds complexity. So you keep them in one service when strong consistency genuinely matters, for example keeping the debit and credit of a single internal ledger posting together, and you accept sagas only across boundaries where eventual consistency is fine.

Decompose by scalability splits out a component whose load profile differs sharply from the rest. If the fraud-scoring component needs ten times the CPU of everything else during peak, extracting it lets you scale just that service. In practice you combine strategies: start with business capabilities, refine with DDD subdomains, keep strongly-consistent operations together, and carve out scalability hotspots. The senior-level nuance is that the goal is high cohesion and low coupling: a well-decomposed service changes for one reason and talks to others rarely, while a badly decomposed one changes whenever anything changes and chatters constantly over the network.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India must split its monolith and the architects debate where to cut. Problem 1 — someone proposes a "DatabaseService", a "ControllerService", and a "UtilService", which are technical layers, so every feature still spans all three and nothing is independent. This is exactly why we decompose by business capability instead. Problem 2 — the word "account" means different things to the deposits team and the lending team, and a single shared model keeps breaking. This is exactly the DDD subdomain strategy: separate bounded contexts. Problem 3 — fraud scoring spikes to ten times normal load at peak and drags everything down. This is exactly the scalability strategy: extract it.

The mini-project models a small `DecompositionPlanner` that classifies proposed boundaries as good or bad, a `BusinessCapability` enum for Payments, Lending, and Fraud, and a `ScalabilityProfile` that flags a hotspot. A runnable demo rejects a technical-layer split, accepts capability-based services, and flags fraud scoring for independent scaling.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: a proposed "DatabaseService" boundary, the four business capabilities, and load multipliers for Payment (3x) and Fraud (10x).

Step 1: The planner evaluates "DatabaseService". It matches a known technical-layer name, so it is rejected as a bad cut because every feature would still span it.

Step 2: The planner evaluates each business capability: Payments, Lending, Fraud Detection, and Notification. None is a technical layer, so each is accepted as a good boundary mapping to a capability the bank actually offers.

Step 3: The scalability profile evaluates the Payment Service with a peak multiplier of 3. Because it is below the threshold of 5, it does not need to be split purely for scaling; it can scale as part of its normal service footprint.

Step 4: The scalability profile evaluates the Fraud Detection Service with a peak multiplier of 10. This is far above the threshold, so it is flagged for extraction so it can scale to ten instances without forcing the quieter services to grow.

Step 5: The final plan combines strategies: capability-based services for clear ownership, DDD subdomains to keep the ubiquitous language consistent, strongly-consistent operations kept together, and fraud scoring carved out as a scalability hotspot.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Decomposition pattern is the set of strategies for deciding where to draw service boundaries, and the whole goal is high cohesion inside a service and low coupling between services. I use four strategies together. The first and most important is decomposing by business capability: each service owns something the business actually does, such as Payments, Lending, or Notifications at National Bank of India. This boundary is stable because capabilities change slowly, and ownership is clear because one team can own payments end to end. I always warn against the opposite mistake of decomposing by technical layer into a ControllerService and a DatabaseService, because then every feature still spans every service and nothing is independent.

The second strategy refines the first using Domain-Driven Design subdomains. A bounded context is a region where a term has one precise meaning, so "account" means a loan account in the Lending context and a savings account in the Deposits context. Giving each bounded context its own service keeps the ubiquitous language consistent and avoids one giant shared model that tries to mean everything to everyone.

The third strategy is decomposing by transaction. If two pieces of data must always change together under one consistency boundary, I keep them in one service, because splitting them forces a saga and eventual consistency. So I keep a single ledger posting's debit and credit together and accept sagas only where eventual consistency is genuinely acceptable. The fourth strategy is decomposing by scalability: when one component has a sharply different load profile, like fraud scoring spiking to ten times normal at peak, I extract it so it scales to many instances without forcing the quieter services to grow with it.

In practice I combine all four: I start with business capabilities, refine with DDD subdomains, keep strongly-consistent operations together, and carve out scalability hotspots. The test I apply to every boundary is whether the resulting service changes for one reason and talks to others rarely. If it changes whenever anything changes and chatters constantly over the network, the cut was wrong and I redraw it.
